newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch prince groomed for future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch prince groomed for future.

text.p: Prince Willem Alexander of the Netherlands is being groomed for his role as king with a crash course in industry and a string of high-profile public engagements.

Once the darling of the Dutch tabloids because of his love of fast cars and good-looking women, the eldest son of Queen Beatrix, who turns 30 on Sunday, spends more time these days touring factories than publicly living it up.
"He's doing what his mother and every other Dutch monarch-to-be did before him -- preparing for the task that lies ahead," says a government aide.

But after a year spent swotting up on matters of state, now followed by several months of getting to know industry from the inside, the prince's biggest hurdle to gaining the throne may well be finding a suitable consort.

"Willem Alexander will be expected to marry and enjoy family life before ascending to the throne, like his mother and grandmother did," says one royal watcher. "He won't become king for at least 10 years yet."
Queen Beatrix married at 28 and raised a family of three boys in relative privacy before succeeding her mother Juliana in 1981 when she was 43.
PRESSURE TO MARRY
Juliana, too, married in her late twenties and with these royal precedents the pressure is on Willem Alexander -- known as Alex to his friends -- to settle down and start a family.

But after the media furore unleashed several years ago by the prince's public admission that he was seeing blonde law student -- now KLM Royal Dutch Airlines staffer -- Emily Bremers, all has gone quiet on the subject of his love life.
Some paparazzi swear the romance is still going strong, pointing to the couple's attendance at a recent pop concert, but others believe the prince is on his own again.
"It's becoming noticeable that...(Emily) is never around when the crown prince is out enjoying himself," the weekly Weekend commented in an article several months ago.
"I'm assuming it's still on, given that we have never been informed it's off," countered a royal reporter who declined to be named.

The spectre of the British royal family's widely publicised marriage difficulties will have prompted Queen Beatrix -- always a highly private person -- to counsel even more circumspection than usual, he said.
"One thing is for sure -- Alex will never let himself be dragooned into marriage before he's ready, he's too stubborn for that."

He characterised Willem Alexander as easygoing and friendly, with a well-developed sense of humour -- an important asset in the face of often sniping media commentary on the stocky prince's weight, his interests and his intellectual capabilities.
"(He has) the profundity of a surfboard and all the intellectual aura of a tossed salad," the Dutch business weekly Elsevier quoted one commentator as saying in its latest issue.
Others have compared him unfavourably to his studious mother, pointing to the six years he took to complete a four-year history degree at Leiden University and his frequent skiing and boating trips.
"All those stories saying he is this and he is that, what I know of him is that he is seriously applying himself to preparing for kingship," says the royal reporter.

"A lot of the misunderstanding arises from the fact that he likes to keep his private life private -- people don't know him, so they speculate. He is a bright, socially adept young man who will make a very good king."
BID TO TRANSFORM IMAGE

In recent years Willem Alexander has embarked on a busy calendar of official engagements, state and foreign visits seemingly calculated to transform his image from playboy prince into serious-minded king-in-waiting.

He is increasingly taking over from his mother at public events, travelling to St Petersburg to officiate at the opening of celebrations commemorating three centuries of Russian-Dutch ties, visiting Dutch troops serving with the United Nations force in Bosnia and the first joint German-Dutch troop unit in Muenster.
But his attempt to overhaul his image has had its setbacks.

His dance of joy with the Dutch Olympic women's hockey team after their win in Atlanta and his equally exuberant welcome for the Dutch rowing gold medallists in defiance of Olympic protocol prompted a long-running debate in the serious Dutch press about his behaviour.
"Do we want a prince who jigs up and down with the winning team like any vulgar fan?" asked the evening broadsheet NRC Handelsblad.

The answer came back as a resounding 'yes' in a subsequent survey conducted by one of the country's largest pollsters, with 80 percent of respondents saying they did not consider Willem Alexander's behaviour inappropriate.
"He's a wonderful spontaneous chap -- an ideal king for the 21st century," says Leo van Maaren, chairman of the newly-formed Willem Alexander Fan club (WAF).

A poll conducted this month by the royalist-inclined newspaper Trouw indicated many Dutch agree. Some 80 percent of respondents believe the monarchy should stay, with 65 percent saying 59-year-old Queen Beatrix should abdicate in favour of her son when she turns 65.
"That's not likely," said another member of the royal press corps. "Beatrix enjoys the job far too much and Willem Alexander will just have to wait."
